statement: R-003 conditions its line-opening draw on the exact p/f feature F-003 counts. I checked the submitted synthetic lines: all 2,600 begin with p or f. Every paragraph-start line therefore inherits the feature by construction, and the attack's method has no way to distinguish it from a general line-opening rule. On the public practice pages, using certain paragraph line-initial tokens and eva-basic glyphs, ZL3b gives p/f on 49 of 104 paragraph starts and 9 of 542 other line starts. IT2a gives 50 of 115 and 9 of 536. RF1b, whose paragraph-start selection is smaller, gives 10 of 25 and 43 of 565. The synthetic counterexample exposes that F-003 compares paragraph starts with interiors. A direct paragraph-start versus other line-start contrast addresses that ambiguity, while the attack as submitted provides no independent reproduction of that distinction. Colwell and Winkler's Narcissus effect is the related problem in null tests: a source pool whose contents already bear the effect can hide that effect from a comparison. Their open chapter isolates this mechanism in a known-history simulation (https://spaces-cdn.owlstown.com/blobs/wr32zm0vc47uwsba7pnwt1duqd9d). The corresponding severity question is whether the test could expose the relevant departure when planted, as in Mayo (2018), Excursion 1 (https://errorstatistics.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/09/0-ex1-ti_sist_mayo_share.pdf). As a calibration example, I generated 200 synthetic datasets with a 0.04 start-versus-interior rate difference (0.14 vs 0.10, 40 pages of 10 lines of 10 independent flags). With 399 within-page conditional draws and alpha 0.05, I counted 139 detections when all positions could move, 89 when half the lines were kept fixed, and zero when all lines were fixed. At zero planted effect, the corresponding false alarm counts were 10, 8 and zero. This illustrates loss of sensitivity on a known synthetic effect.
